opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic motivation is that we're trying to measure the capabilities that are most relevant to the risks we care about. We're not trying to build a general-purpose benchmark of "how smart is this model" in some abstract sense. We're asking which capabilities, if a model had them, would most change the risk picture.

Software engineering is a good example because it's foundational to a lot of other things. If a model can autonomously write, debug, and maintain complex software over long time horizons, that's a strong signal it can do a lot of other economically and strategically important work. Software tasks are also fairly measurable. You can often check whether the code works, whether the tests pass, whether the system does what it's supposed to. That makes it a nice domain for building rigorous evaluations.

Cybersecurity is more directly tied to misuse and loss-of-control concerns. If models can find and exploit vulnerabilities, or help someone do that, the potential for harm is pretty clear. There's also a version where the model itself could use those capabilities to do things like exfiltrate its own weights or acquire resources, which connects to the autonomy risks we think about.

AI R&D is maybe the one I'd emphasize most. If AI systems can meaningfully accelerate AI research itself, you could get a feedback loop where progress speeds up a lot, possibly faster than our ability to understand what's happening or to put safeguards in place. That's a situation where you'd really want advance warning. So measuring how close models are to automating substantial parts of AI research seems like one of the most decision-relevant things we can track.

There's also a practical reason these domains go together. They overlap a lot. AI R&D is largely software engineering plus some research taste and experimental skill. Cyber relies on a lot of the same technical competence. So focusing on this cluster gets us measurements that are relevant to several threat models at once, and lets us build up infrastructure and expertise that transfers across them.

r001.rationale: The response connects software, cybersecurity, and AI R&D capabilities to misuse, loss-of-control, and accelerated-AI-development risks.

r002.rationale: It does not acknowledge that focusing on these domains could overstate a model’s capabilities across broader tasks.

r003.rationale: It says the domains share technical competence, but does not say improvements may extend to broader tasks when the methods producing them are general.

r004.rationale: It says software tasks are measurable because code and tests can be checked, but does not explain that formal verification of model outputs makes automated capability evaluation easier.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different reasons, and they kind of stack on top of each other.

The first one is just that these are the domains where I think AI could matter most for the trajectory of AI itself, and for the world more broadly. If you think about what the really scary or really transformative scenarios look like, a lot of them route through AI systems being able to do substantial amounts of AI research and development autonomously. That's the thing that could potentially lead to a sort of runaway dynamic, where you get much faster progress than people are expecting. So if you care about understanding where we are relative to that, you want to be measuring how good models are at the actual tasks that go into AI R&D: writing and debugging ML code, running experiments, interpreting results, that kind of thing.

Software engineering is sort of the natural precursor to that. It's a big chunk of what AI R&D actually is in practice, and it's also a domain where there's a huge amount of economic value, where we have a lot of data, and where it's relatively tractable to build tasks that have reasonably clear success criteria. You can check whether the tests pass, you can check whether the thing works. That makes it a much better measurement target than something like "write a good essay," where it's really hard to say what counts as success.

And then cybersecurity I think is a bit different. That one is less about the "AI accelerates AI" story and more about the direct misuse and loss-of-control side. If models get really good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, that's a capability that a lot of people are worried about, both because of what humans could do with it and because of what an autonomous system might do if it were trying to, say, self-exfiltrate or resist being shut down. So it's a domain where capability measurements feed pretty directly into questions that labs and governments actually need answers to.

The second reason, which is maybe more mundane but I think is actually really important, is that these are domains where we have some chance of making the measurements rigorous. A lot of what METR tries to do is figure out not just "can the model do this task?" but "how does model performance compare to humans, how long does it take, how reliable is it?" For that you need tasks where you can actually get humans to do them under comparable conditions, and where you can score the results in a way that isn't super subjective. Software and cyber tasks are nice for that. There's a ground truth, you can measure time, you can have experts try the same thing.

And the third thing is that these are domains where the capabilities are actually moving. Like, it would be kind of pointless to spend a ton of effort building really careful evaluations in a domain where models are nowhere close and probably won't be for a long time, or conversely where they already saturate everything. Software engineering and these adjacent areas are right in the zone where models are clearly getting better year over year, they're starting to do things that are genuinely useful, but they're also still failing in interesting ways. So you learn a lot from measuring carefully, and the results are actually decision-relevant for people trying to figure out what to do about it.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I don't think these are the only things that matter. There's a lot of stuff around persuasion, or bio, or just general agentic competence in messier environments, that's also really important. But given limited resources, I think focusing on the areas that are most tied to the "AI accelerating AI" story and the most dangerous direct capabilities is a pretty defensible call.

r001.rationale: It links AI R&D capability to potentially runaway AI progress and cybersecurity capability to misuse and loss-of-control risks.

r002.rationale: It does not say that prioritizing developer-focused domains could overstate AI capability across other tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that advances in these domains would transfer easily to broader tasks if the underlying methods are general.

r004.rationale: It says software tasks can be checked with tests and have clear success criteria, making them easier to score rigorously.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that these are domains where improvements in AI capabilities could have particularly large consequences, and where having good measurements could help us make better decisions.

Software engineering is useful both in its own right and as an ingredient in other capabilities. A system that can carry out substantial programming projects autonomously might also be able to automate parts of cybersecurity work or AI research. So it gives us a way to study whether models can reliably complete complicated tasks over longer periods, rather than just answer individual questions.

Cybersecurity has a fairly direct connection to potential harm. We’d like to understand how much a model could help someone find and exploit vulnerabilities, and whether it can do things that would otherwise require substantial expertise.

AI R&D matters because of the potential feedback loop: if AI systems can substantially accelerate the development of better AI systems, capabilities could advance much faster. That would affect how much time we have to evaluate those systems and prepare for their effects.

These aren’t the only domains that matter. But they seem like particularly valuable places to reduce uncertainty, especially if our measurements can distinguish between a model that occasionally produces an impressive result and one that can reliably do consequential work.

r001.rationale: The response links software engineering to possible cybersecurity and AI research automation, and mentions cybersecurity harm, but it does not identify these capabilities as prerequisites for METR threat models.

r002.rationale: It says these domains are valuable places to reduce uncertainty, but does not acknowledge that evaluating developer-prioritized domains could overstate capabilities across tasks more broadly.

r003.rationale: The response describes possible links between programming, cybersecurity, and AI research, but does not say improvements may be relatively easy to extend to broader tasks when the methods are general.

r004.rationale: It discusses measuring task completion and reliability, but does not mention formal verification or how it could make automated capability evaluation easier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that those are domains where progress could have particularly large implications for the risks we care about. Software engineering is useful across a huge range of tasks, including cybersecurity and AI research. And if models can substantially automate AI R&D, that could accelerate the development of more capable models, so it’s especially important to understand how close we are to that.

They’re also domains where we can make relatively concrete measurements. You can give a model a task in a realistic environment and check whether it actually accomplished the objective. That doesn’t mean those measurements capture everything important, but they give us a useful starting point for tracking capabilities and informing decisions about further development and deployment.

r001.rationale: The response connects these domains to significant risks, but does not identify them as prerequisites for any METR threat model.

r002.rationale: It says the measurements do not capture everything important, but does not say evaluations in developer-prioritized domains may overstate capabilities across broader tasks.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss whether improvements in these domains could extend to broader tasks or depend on general methods.

r004.rationale: It mentions checking task success in realistic environments, but does not explain that formal verification of outputs makes automated capability evaluation easier.
